Compactness. A topological property that generalizes the familiar finiteness of closed intervals to arbitrary spaces. A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. This seemingly abstract condition has profound consequences: continuous functions on compact spaces achieve their maximum and minimum values, and compact spaces are well-behaved in surprising ways.

A topological space is compact if every open cover—a collection of open sets whose union is the entire space—admits a finite subcover. No infinite collection of open sets is necessary to cover a compact space. Closed intervals in the real numbers are compact. Open intervals are not, because the endpoints escape. Finite unions of compact sets are compact.

The Heine-Borel theorem states that in Euclidean space, a set is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. This classical result fails in infinite-dimensional spaces. Continuous images of compact spaces are compact: if f is continuous and the domain is compact, then the image is also compact. Compactness is topologically preserved.

The extreme value theorem states that a continuous function on a compact space attains its maximum and minimum values—unlike on open intervals, where suprema may be unattained. Hausdorff spaces, including Euclidean spaces, separate distinct points with disjoint open sets. Compact Hausdorff spaces are normal, able to separate disjoint closed sets with disjoint open neighborhoods.

Compactness ensures convergence: in compact metric spaces, every sequence has a convergent subsequence, by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem. Compact sets behave like generalized finite sets with finiteness-like properties. Tychonoff's theorem states that an arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology—surprising because infinite products of non-compact spaces can be non-compact. Sequential compactness, where every sequence has a convergent subsequence, is equivalent to compactness in metric spaces but weaker in general topological spaces.
